{"id": "100:8/q02", "question": "What does al-khayr mean here?", "turns_on": "Whether khayr is confined to wealth, extends to worldly advantage or chosen desire, or retains its broader moral sense; context and other Qurʾanic usages are cited.", "positions": [{"id": "100:8/q02/p1", "position": "Wealth or money.", "reasons": "Reported from Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, Qatāda, ʿIkrima, and Ibn Zayd; ʿIkrima or Qatāda generalize this sense to every Qurʾanic khayr. Many cite 2:180, Rāzī also 70:21. Qurṭubī adduces ʿAdī's poetry. Bint al-Shāṭiʾ accepts wealth in this context because an ungrateful witness would love money rather than virtue, while qualifying broad lexical claims. Kur'an Yolu specifies abundant wealth; al-Ālūsī reports that limitation for 2:180. Ibn al-Jawzī lists worldly wealth as a fifteenth sense."}, {"id": "100:8/q02/p2", "position": "Worldly life and its desired advantages, including wealth, health, status, power, or pleasures.", "reasons": "Ibn Zayd is reported as taking khayr as worldly life. Ibn ʿAṭiyya adds health and favor with rulers because disbelievers and the ignorant recognize only worldly goods; Study Quran points to 3:14. Quṭb traces worldly wealth, power, and pleasure to self-love without faith. Ṭabarī's Ibn Zayd still cites the bequest verse for wealth."}, {"id": "100:8/q02/p3", "position": "Whatever the person chooses for himself.", "reasons": "Māwardī offers chosen preference as a third possibility, so the person strongly loves his own selection."}, {"id": "100:8/q02/p4", "position": "Good deeds or benefits from God, toward which the person remains constricted.", "reasons": "The Kashshāf's further reading makes good deeds the object; al-Ālūsī says these come from God and describes an unresponsive person. Elmalılı prefers the reading of aversion to good works that cost money or bodily effort."}, {"id": "100:8/q02/p5", "position": "Good in a broad sense, which people naturally love but mistake worldly ornaments for.", "reasons": "Ṭabāṭabāʾī prefers this wider sense and connects the mistake with forgetting gratitude. Rāghib, as reported by Kur'an Yolu, includes reason, justice, virtue, and benefit. Bint al-Shāṭiʾ surveys about 125 comparative uses of better/best, contrasts with evil in 17:11, 10:11, 21:35 and 70:21, and with harm in 7:188, 6:17 and 10:107; she also notes horses in 38:32 and wealth in 23:55–56."}, {"id": "100:8/q02/p6", "position": "Worldly loves falsely called good by their adherents; true good is freedom from creation and obedience to God.", "reasons": "Tustarī contrasts the conventional label for love of self, the world, and desire with neediness toward God and fulfilling His command."}]}
{"id": "100:8/q03", "question": "Why is wealth called good?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "100:8/q03/p1", "position": "It follows people's customary valuation of wealth, even when the wealth is illicit or harmful in the final outcome.", "reasons": "Ibn Zayd compares 2:180 and people's naming of battle or its wounds as evil despite 3:174. Wāḥidī says the label reflects ordinary usage rather than ultimate outcome. Rāzī cites 70:21 too. Bursawī and al-Ālūsī stress that illicit or afterlife-harmful wealth can still be called good; Elmalılı says the false belief that wealth is wholly good is condemned. Biqāʿī points to its immediate visible benefit, which distracts from unseen service of God."}]}
{"id": "100:8/q04", "question": "How does li-ḥubb al-khayr relate grammatically to shadīd?", "turns_on": "Whether lām is causal, marks a domain of strength, or participates in an omitted and reordered 'love'; opponents of inversion say the surface construction is sound.", "positions": [{"id": "100:8/q04/p1", "position": "The lām is causal: because of love of wealth, the person is miserly or severe.", "reasons": "Al-Khaṭṭābī, Ibn al-Anbārī, al-Samīn, al-Suyūṭī, Biqāʿī, al-Ālūsī, and Ibn ʿĀshūr give the sense 'because of'; Ibn al-Anbārī says this plain wording makes inversion unnecessary. Burhān glosses min ajl. Abū Ḥayyān explicitly rejects an ellipsis on this analysis. Al-Samīn says there is no need to make the lām mean ʿalā."}, {"id": "100:8/q04/p2", "position": "The lām marks the domain or capacity of strength: he is strong in loving wealth.", "reasons": "Al-Samīn says shadīd li-shayʾ can mean capable of it; Abū Ḥayyān says a strong person can manage and master an affair. Al-Ālūsī prefers the sense 'in' for the lām with strong love; Quṭrub compares 'much striking for Zayd.' Ibn al-Āshūr's Biqāʿī notes that shadīd cannot simply govern the following love phrase across the lām and requires an understood complement."}, {"id": "100:8/q04/p3", "position": "The order is understood as 'strong in love of wealth,' with a repeated 'love' omitted after shadīd.", "reasons": "Al-Farrāʾ and Kufan grammarians say the first ḥubb supplies the omitted second occurrence; this also preserves verse endings. They compare 14:18, where 'wind' is understood after a 'stormy day'; al-Ālūsī's fuller citation gives 41:16. Ibn Qutayba and Burhān report inversion. Al-Khaṭṭābī records the objection that ordinary speakers say they are intense in love of someone or something. Ibn Qutayba himself objects to imposing inversion without grounds, noting poetic reversals may arise from error, rhyme, meter, or necessity; Ibn al-Anbārī objects that the surface wording already works."}, {"id": "100:8/q04/p4", "position": "An analysis shifts an adjective connected to a raised verbal noun and fronts its predicate complement.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī reports this proposal but objects that the predicate complement cannot precede it."}, {"id": "100:8/q04/p5", "position": "Some take the lām to mean ʿalā.", "reasons": "Al-Samīn reports this but sees no need for it."}]}
{"id": "100:8/q05", "question": "What does shadīd say about the person's love and conduct?", "turns_on": "Whether shadīd names stinginess, the intensity of love, energetic worldly pursuit, constriction toward good, or physical strength; Arabic miser terminology, poetry, and the lām's syntax distinguish them.", "positions": [{"id": "100:8/q05/p1", "position": "He is miserly, tightly withholding wealth because he loves it.", "reasons": "Arabic calls a miser shadīd, mutashaddid, or shadīda; Ṭarafa's line depicts death selecting a grasping miser's choice wealth. Thaʿlabī and Qurṭubī also cite fāḥish/fāḥisha for a miser in 2:268. Al-Ḥasan specifies withholding God's due. Al-Ālūsī gives passive 'held back from generosity' and active 'tying the purse shut.' Ibn ʿĀshūr adds Abū Dhuʾayb's elegy (with jawl meaning earth), 59:9 on protection from stinginess, and charity withheld despite ostentatious spending; Ibn Kathīr accepts this with the strong-love reading."}, {"id": "100:8/q05/p2", "position": "He intensely loves wealth; the strength describes the love itself.", "reasons": "Al-Farrāʾ prefers intense love and an implied second ḥubb. Māwardī says love is strong and increasing; Qurṭubī and Abū Ḥayyān take this as the direct sense. Ibn Kathīr accepts both this and the miserly sense; al-Ālūsī prefers powerful love. Bint al-Shāṭiʾ notes that the comparative ashad ordinarily expresses force, with the exceptional love of believers for God at 2:165."}, {"id": "100:8/q05/p3", "position": "He is strong and capable in pursuing or acquiring worldly wealth but weak in worship and gratitude.", "reasons": "Zamakhsharī, Rāzī, Nasafī, Abū Ḥayyān, Biqāʿī, Bursawī, and Elmalılı contrast worldly energy with neglect of God; Abū Ḥayyān explains strength for an affair as mastery of it. Biqāʿī adds that love of good ought to produce gratefulness and increase."}, {"id": "100:8/q05/p4", "position": "He is constricted or closed toward good things or good deeds, refusing generous, expansive action.", "reasons": "Zamakhsharī's further gloss describes a person withdrawn and tightfisted; his fuller reading allows good deeds. Rāzī repeats the constricted rather than generous description of love of wealth. Qāshānī applies the constriction to good leading to truth. Elmalılı prefers the Kashshāf's reading of aversion to works requiring money or exertion."}, {"id": "100:8/q05/p5", "position": "He is strong in physical powers.", "reasons": "Al-Naḥḥās transmits this alternative gloss of shadīd al-quwā."}]}
{"id": "100:8/q06", "question": "What do the word's root and Qurʾanic usage add to shadīd here?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "100:8/q06/p1", "position": "Its basic force is tight binding and strength; frequent Qurʾanic use in threats adds menace to the rebuke of stinginess.", "reasons": "Bint al-Shāṭiʾ traces shadd to a knot or binding, citing 47:4, 10:88, 76:28, 20:31, 28:35, and 38:20; maturity formulas appear in 6:152, 17:34, 12:22, 28:14, 40:67, 46:15, 18:82, and 22:5. She counts roughly forty shadīd uses for punishment, divine might, seizure, or afterlife retribution; exceptions involve iron (57:25), Lot's hoped-for support (11:80), Solomon's threat (27:21), and fighting forces (17:5, 27:33, 48:16, 72:8). Ashadd denotes severity or force, and only 2:165 uses it for love. Against the prior self-witness, the threatening association intensifies the indictment."}]}
{"id": "100:8/q07", "question": "Why place li-ḥubb al-khayr before la-shadīd?", "turns_on": "Whether the fronting belongs to a plain causal phrase or to a reordered phrase with a repeated word omitted; both explanations mention the verse ending.", "positions": [{"id": "100:8/q07/p1", "position": "Fronting highlights the surprising motive, love of wealth, and preserves the verse's cadence.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr says the causal phrase is fronted for emphasis and rhyme; a governed genitive phrase can precede a predicate with lām, as in verse 6, despite lām al-ibtidāʾ's usual precedence. Biqāʿī says shadīd cannot govern the following phrase across the lām and points to an omitted governed element."}, {"id": "100:8/q07/p2", "position": "The rearrangement and omission of repeated ḥubb keep the verse endings aligned.", "reasons": "Al-Farrāʾ and Kufan

{"id": "100:8/q08", "question": "How does this clause relate to the witness clause before it?", "turns_on": "The referent of the witness in verse 7 and whether that clause interrupts the syntax or completes the description of human self-testimony.", "positions": [{"id": "100:8/q08/p1", "position": "The human's ingratitude and love of wealth are stated together, with God's witness to that condition placed between them.", "reasons": "Ṭabarī says verse 7 is semantically delayed or parenthetic between verses 6 and 8; Qatāda says God witnesses specifically the human's intense love of wealth. Qushayrī reports that God may witness his condition; Durّ reports Mujāhid for God as witness. Al-Suyūṭī notes a rare shift from human to Lord and back. Bint al-Shāṭiʾ objects to interpretations that switch the pronoun to the human in the next verse and break the unity of the three verses."}, {"id": "100:8/q08/p2", "position": "The human himself witnesses his ingratitude or his hoarded possessions, and the new clause exposes its motive.", "reasons": "Qushayrī reports the human's own hoards as witness; Ibn ʿAbbās is reported for the human in verse 7. Biqāʿī finds it astonishing that a person denies the benefactor while testifying against himself; Corpus Coranicum reads public witness to ingratitude and possessiveness. Ibn ʿĀshūr says the clauses reveal variable ingratitude in speech, intention, conduct, or neglect."}]}
{"id": "100:8/q09", "question": "What conduct or motive does love of wealth expose?", "turns_on": "Which practical or spiritual consequence the verse's attachment to wealth is used to explain.", "positions": [{"id": "100:8/q09/p1", "position": "It drives ingratitude, hoarding, withheld charity, and preference for immediate possessions over service of God.", "reasons": "Biqāʿī says the visible present benefit eclipses unseen afterlife benefit. Ibn ʿĀshūr cites 59:9 and Sūrat al-Fajr 89:18–20: Arabs condemned stinginess yet neglected the poor and orphans while spending for reputation, drinking, and gambling. Elmalılı urges spending for good works and preparing force for God's cause (8:60); Bursawī's Persian verses urge giving rather than leaving regretted treasure to heirs. Islahi compares the obedient horse returning spoils and accepting feed with man boasting like Qārūn (28:78). Corpus Coranicum links love of possessions with 89:20, 76:8, and 75:20."}, {"id": "100:8/q09/p2", "position": "For hypocrites, greed can explain outward profession of faith to protect property and gain spoils.", "reasons": "Bursawī takes the placement after ingratitude as a hint at this motive."}, {"id": "100:8/q09/p3", "position": "Without faith, excessive self-love fixes ambition on wealth, power, and pleasures; faith makes generosity and higher values possible.", "reasons": "Quṭb says unbelieving ambition is earthbound and limited by lifespan; connection to God and the Hereafter joins earthly life to the eternal Origin and End, replacing ingratitude and greed with gratitude, generosity, and mercy. Islahi says God the benefactor is worthier of love, and believers prefer Him over self-interest, as in 2:165. Ibn ʿAṭiyya says love of afterlife good is praiseworthy and may lead to success; Ṭabāṭabāʾī says mistaking worldly ornaments for good causes forgotten gratitude."}]}
{"id": "100:8/q10", "question": "What inward reading is drawn from the attachment to good?", "turns_on": "Which divine gift is mistakenly treated as one's own and hoarded.", "positions": [{"id": "100:8/q10/p1", "position": "The self is veiled by divine favors, stopping at gifts instead of using them to reach God.", "reasons": "Bursawī reports al-Qāshānī on ingratitude; Qāshānī also sees love of wealth as hoarding and veiling or constriction toward good leading to truth. Tustarī says worldly loves are conventionally called good while genuine good is independence from creatures, need for God, and obedience."}, {"id": "100:8/q10/p2", "position": "Ingratitude means claiming independent possession of existence and divine attributes and hoarding guidance.", "reasons": "Bursawī reports al-Taʾwīlāt al-Najmiyya: one misuses these gifts or refuses to share guidance."}]}
{"id": "100:8/q11", "question": "What rhetorical pattern does this verse make with its neighbors?", "turns_on": "Different commentators identify distinct sound and discourse devices rather than dispute a single device.", "positions": [{"id": "100:8/q11/p1", "position": "Balanced verse endings and the near sounds shahīd and shadīd form paronomasia.", "reasons": "Bāqillānī calls the passage tarsīʿ with tajnīs and compares 7:201, 68:3, 52:1–2, and 79:3–4. Burhān defines a close-letter type by one changed letter and cites 75:22, 6:26, 44:29, and 4:83. Itqān calls shahīd/shadīd jinās al-lāḥiq, whose differing letters are non-neighboring, with hamaza/lamaza and other pairs."}, {"id": "100:8/q11/p2", "position": "The forceful rhythm suits the dust, opened graves and hearts, and indictment of ingratitude and greed.", "reasons": "Quṭb describes the sūrah's rough, rumbling, cracking sound and rapid jumps before its final settling, like a runner reaching the finish."}, {"id": "100:8/q11/p3", "position": "A shift of pronouns moves from the human to his Lord and back to the human.", "reasons": "Itqān transmits Ibn Abī al-Iṣbaʿ's classification as a rare pronoun shift after mentioning two subjects."}]}
{"id": "100:8/q12", "question": "What role does the verse play in the sūrah's sequence?", "turns_on": "Whether the focus is structural placement, cultural characterization, or the contrast with the opening horses.", "positions": [{"id": "100:8/q12/p1", "position": "Verses 6–8 form the central human indictment, pausing the energetic oath before the final eschatological reckoning.", "reasons": "Corpus Coranicum says these are the sūrah's only nominal sentences, contrasting with surrounding verbal and participial clauses; the ʾinsān saying delays resolution of the enigmatic oath. Neuwirth calls the saying a motif later becoming a topos. Quṭb marks a second scene moving from the charge to ingratitude, denial, selfishness, and miserliness. Corpus Coranicum compares the subsequent accusation-to-doom sequence with Q104 and Old Testament doom prophecy; it sees similar riddling tension in Q90, Q97, Q101 and Q104."}, {"id": "100:8/q12/p2", "position": "The human accusation can be read against pre-Islamic human-centered values.", "reasons": "Corpus Coranicum reports Neuwirth's view, while its author says the text itself does not explicitly attack particular pre-Islamic Arab virtues."}, {"id": "100:8/q12/p3", "position": "The obedient horse's return of spoils exposes the human's refusal to acknowledge his benefactor.", "reasons": "Islahi contrasts the horse accepting its master's feed with man hoarding blessings as self-achieved and boasting like Qārūn in 28:78."}]}
{"id": "100:8/q13", "question": "What is reported about the sūrah's place of revelation?", "turns_on": "The competing reports of Meccan origin and a Medinan raid setting.", "positions": [{"id": "100:8/q13/p1", "position": "It is Meccan.", "reasons": "Jishumī transmits this from al-Ḥasan, ʿIkrima, and Qatāda; Quṭb describes the sūrah as Meccan and counts eleven verses."}, {"id": "100:8/q13/p2", "position": "It is Medinan and connected with a raid.", "reasons": "Jishumī reports this alternative without further details."}]}
{"id": "100:8/q14", "question": "What reward is reported for reciting this sūrah?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "100:8/q14/p1", "position": "Ten good deeds per person who spent the night at Muzdalifah and witnessed Jamʿ.", "reasons": "Jishumī and the Kashshāf transmit the prophetic report; Rāzī's fuller text attributes it to Ubayy and raises it to the Prophet, describing the reward by that number."}]}
{"id": "100:8/q15", "question": "What pilgrimage interpretation is reported for the opening scene?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "100:8/q15/p1", "position": "It depicts departure from ʿArafa, fires, dawn departure from Muzdalifah, a valley floor, and arrival at Mina's Jamʿ.", "reasons": "Al-Durr reports this sequence from Muḥammad ibn Kaʿb al-Quraẓī."}]}
{"id": "100:8/q16", "question": "What is said about the following sūrah's revelation?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "100:8/q16/p1", "position": "Sūrat al-Qāriʿah is Meccan according to all authorities cited.", "reasons": "Māwardī's full text reports this for the next sūrah."}]}

{"id": "107:1/q02", "question": "Is an address kāf added to arāʾayta?", "turns_on": "Whether the transmitted form includes an address marker after the verb.", "positions": [{"id": "107:1/q02/p1", "position": "The received form has no extra address kāf.", "reasons": "Al-Farrāʾ says adding or omitting kāf leaves the meaning unchanged; al-Naḥḥās calls the standard form clear."}, {"id": "107:1/q02/p2", "position": "A reading adds an emphatic second-person kāf: arāʾaytaka.", "reasons": "Attributed to ʿAbd Allāh or Ibn Masʿūd by al-Farrāʾ, al-Naḥḥās, al-Zamakhsharī, al-Rāzī and others, with 17:62 cited as a parallel. Abū Ḥayyān and al-Samīn say the kāf supports the 'tell me' sense because it does not attach to literal seeing; al-Ālūsī contests an absolute ban after figurative seeing."}]}
{"id": "107:1/q03", "question": "What does the opening question do?", "turns_on": "Whether the interrogation seeks recognition, expresses wonder, invokes sight, or asks for an account; several sources combine these functions.", "positions": [{"id": "107:1/q03/p1", "position": "It draws the listener to identify or recognize the denier through the following conduct.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī, al-Rāzī and al-Nasafī paraphrase 'do you know who?' and identify the orphan-pusher in 107:2. Ibn ʿAṭiyya says it recalls anyone with the traits; al-Ālūsī says believers need to recognize and avoid them. Al-Rāghib, via Bint al-Shāṭiʾ, says every Qurʾānic araʾayta alerts the hearer; Muḥammad ʿAbduh says it flags something obscure. The Corpus Coranicum compares 96:9–13 and 53:33–34."}, {"id": "107:1/q03/p2", "position": "It expresses astonishment and rebuke at denial and its surprising moral consequences.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī compares asking why someone exposed himself to danger. Al-Bayḍāwī, al-Ālūsī, Ibn ʿĀshūr, Elmalılı, Iṣlāḥī and Kur'an Yolu stress wonder; Ibn ʿĀshūr says common denial creates suspense until the shocking orphan abuse. Bint al-Shāṭiʾ says asking what seems obvious sharpens attention; the ordinary information question becomes figurative when the asker knows. Al-Qushayrī notes the rebuke for mistreating orphans."}, {"id": "107:1/q03/p3", "position": "It asks whether the denier has been seen, prompting visual recall.", "reasons": "Al-Naḥḥās and al-Ḥawfī permit literal seeing without ellipsis. Ibn ʿĀshūr portrays notorious deniers and deeds as visibly present. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī allows literal vision or recognition."}, {"id": "107:1/q03/p4", "position": "It functions as 'tell me' or 'inform me.'", "reasons": "Al-Rāghib is cited for this gloss; Abū Ḥayyān, al-Samīn, al-Biqāʿī and al-Ālūsī connect it to a two-object construction, often with an unspoken second object. Ibn Khurūf notes jurists' hypothetical use with a following suspended question."}]}
{"id": "107:1/q04", "question": "Who is addressed by arāʾayta?", "turns_on": "Whether direct address is specific to the Prophet or extends to every capable hearer.", "positions": [{"id": "107:1/q04/p1", "position": "The Prophet Muhammad is directly addressed.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī calls him the community's leader and the one who fully grasps the matter; Elmalılı and al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī extend the address through him to listeners. Al-Rāzī reports this option; Bursevî has the Prophet asked."}, {"id": "107:1/q04/p2", "position": "Any rational or suitable listener is addressed.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī asks why one would risk eternal punishment after clear proofs or trade lasting good for fleeting gain. Ibn ʿAṭiyya asks listeners to recall acquaintances; al-Ālūsī permits anyone fit; Qutb summons anyone able to see. Corpus Coranicum suggests the address may even reach the worshippers later criticized in verses 4–5."}]}
{"id": "107:1/q05", "question": "How does arāʾayta govern the sentence?", "turns_on": "The verb's sense determines whether it needs one object, two objects with an ellipsis, or a later syntactic completion.", "positions": [{"id": "107:1/q05/p1", "position": "It has one object, the relative phrase, as a verb of visual seeing or knowing.", "reasons": "Al-Naḥḥās and al-Ḥawfī say literal seeing needs no ellipsis. Al-Samīn gives one object to visual perception; al-Ālūsī allows knowing with one object. Ibn ʿĀshūr specifically prefers physical vision. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī allows sight or recognition. Al-Ālūsī resists the rule that figurative vision must derive from physical sight."}, {"id": "107:1/q05/p2", "position": "As 'inform me,' it takes two objects; the omitted second asks whether the denier deserves punishment or is right or wrong.", "reasons": "Al-Ḥawfī and al-Biqāʿī supply deserved punishment after the proofs; al-Qurṭubī supplies 'is he right or mistaken?' Abū Ḥayyān says this omitted clause is a second object rather than the answer to the question. The addressee kāf supports the 'inform me' analysis for Abū Ḥayyān and al-Samīn."}, {"id": "107:1/q05/p3", "position": "As 'inform me,' it takes two objects; the omitted second asks who the denier is.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī supplies 'who is he?'; Abū Ḥayyān and al-Samīn report it, while Abū Ḥayyān says it is a second object rather than an independent answer. Al-Ālūsī allows this ellipsis."}, {"id": "107:1/q05/p4", "position": "An alternative coordinates fa-dhālika with the denier and lets later text indicate an omitted answer.", "reasons": "Al-Zamakhsharī proposes accusative coordination and treats later woe to the worshippers as an indication, with a generic singular yielding plural reference. Abū Ḥayyān rejects the parse: the demonstrative points to the same denier, nominative subject is simpler, a second object is confused with an answer, and plural substitution is forced. {"id": "107:1/q07", "question": "What does yukadhdhibu express?", "turns_on": "Whether the form is treated as the ordinary denial verb or as emphasizing repeated conduct.", "positions": [{"id": "107:1/q07/p1", "position": "It means denying or disbelieving the object named after bi.", "reasons": "Bint al-Shāṭiʾ contrasts the wider Arabic kadhib, which includes false appearances, mistaken expectations, sensory error, false dreams or hopes and self-delusion; kadhdhaba bi is explicit denial. Al-Biqāʿī stresses an active rejection of whoever conveys the matter; Ibn ʿĀshūr says the imperfect verb conveys repeated conduct."}, {"id": "107:1/q07/p2", "position": "The imperfect depicts repeated, continuing denial.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr groups 'denies,' 'pushes' and 'urges' as ongoing behavior rather than isolated acts."}]}
{"id": "107:1/q08", "question": "Is the preposition bi retained before al-dīn?", "turns_on": "Whether early parallels with kadhdhaba support the received preposition; al-Ṭabarī says it makes no semantic difference.", "positions": [{"id": "107:1/q08/p1", "position": "The received reading includes bi.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī calls its bāʾ an added particle that does not alter the meaning. {"id": "107:1/q09", "question": "What does al-dīn mean here?", "turns_on": "Whether the immediate context and early Qurʾānic parallels point to eschatological reckoning, or the wider senses of religious belief, law, and scripture.", "positions": [{"id": "107:1/q09/p1", "position": "Reckoning, accounting, and resurrection judgment.", "reasons": "Muqātil, Ibn Jurayj, Mujāhid, ʿIkrima and others gloss it as reckoning; al-Tustarī places the accounting on the day of judgment. Ibn Kathīr includes resurrection. Ibn ʿAṭiyya and others link accounting closely to recompense. Corpus Coranicum favors this early eschatological sense, comparing dīn and yawm al-dīn in 82:9, 95:7 and other passages, and notes an Aramaic dīnā connection."}, {"id": "107:1/q09/p2", "position": "Recompense: reward for good and punishment for evil.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī presents this as a third meaning beside reckoning and God's judgment; al-Ṭabarī, al-Qurṭubī, al-Bayḍāwī, Ibn ʿAṭiyya, al-Ālūsī and others include reward and punishment. Al-Rāzī prefers it with reckoning because resurrection belief can motivate good even in a non-Muslim. Elmalılı cites 95:7 and 99:7–8; Iṣlāḥī cites 1:3; al-Ālūsī quotes the maxim that one is repaid as one acts."}, {"id": "107:1/q09/p3", "position": "God's judgment, command, ordinance, or law.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās is repeatedly reported for this gloss. Ibn al-Jawzī compares the king's law in 12:76. Kur'an Yolu says God's judgment and afterlife judgment entail one another. Al-Ālūsī lists God's command."}, {"id": "107:1/q09/p4", "position": "Religion or Islam, including religious belief and law.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī reports denial of God, prophethood, resurrection or revealed law as included, but elsewhere favors recompense; he argues unqualified dīn in Qurʾānic usage denotes Islam (3:19), since false doctrine follows passion rather than submission. Bint al-Shāṭiʾ prefers Islam, citing 3:19, 39:3, 5:3 and 3:85; the standard professions and rites alone do not establish it. Al-Bayḍāwī, al-Ālūsī and Study Quran allow this sense. Corpus Coranicum reports Birkeland and Nöldeke/Schwally for it but rejects it for this early passage, even while noting later 109:6 and a probably authentic Umayya poem already use the sense."}, {"id": "107:1/q09/p5", "position": "The Qurʾān is the dīn denied.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jawzī records this as an eleventh lexical sense, citing this verse; Abū Ḥayyān and al-Ālūsī also list it."}, {"id": "107:1/q09/p6", "position": "Dīn names the objective validity of religion and moral law.", "reasons": "Asad gives this formulation. Bint al-Shāṭiʾ derives the Arabic word from obedience and submission: madīn is a subjected servant and dayyān can be subduer, judge or ruler."}, {"id": "107:1/q09/p7", "position": "The word also has other Arabic and Qurʾānic senses, without making each the sense of this verse.", "reasons": "Jishumī lists professed way, obedience and custom and calls recompense the root. Bint al-Shāṭiʾ notes fourteen Qurʾānic instances of yawm al-dīn and denial of dīn in 82:9, 95:7 and here. Corpus Coranicum traces a later religious sense to Middle Persian dēn yet notes Umayya's earlier poem, with development beyond a purely linguistic shift."}]}

{"id": "107:1/q18", "question": "Why does denial of recompense lead to bad conduct?", "turns_on": "The notes link belief in final accountability to motives for social and religious duties and infer inner denial from visible behavior.", "positions": [{"id": "107:1/q18/p1", "position": "Without expected reward or punishment, selfish desire and vice lose their restraint.", "reasons": "Al-Wāḥidī's linguistic authorities say denial removes incentives for good and restraints on evil. {"id": "107:1/q21", "question": "How do the opening and later verses fit together?", "turns_on": "Whether the later verses extend one person's portrait or support an alternative grammatical coordination.", "positions": [{"id": "107:1/q21/p1", "position": "The orphan-pusher identified after the opening is the same denier; later vices deepen or mirror the warning.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr says the fāʾ joins denial to pushing the orphan as one person's attributes; the demonstrative builds suspense and fixes attention, whereas plain wording would simply coordinate the acts. {"id": "107:2/q01", "question": "What does the fāʾ in فذلك do?", "turns_on": "Whether the opening question implies a condition, supplies a causal link, or permits a superfluous fāʾ.", "positions": [{"id": "107:2/q01/p1", "position": "It answers an understood condition, such as ‘if you want to know or rebuke the denier.’", "reasons": "Sibawayh supplies ‘if you wanted to rebuke him’; al-Samīn gives ‘if you reflect or seek to know’; al-Ālūsī supplies ‘if you do not know the denier’; Ṭabāṭabāʾī and Elmalılı describe a conditional inference."}, {"id": "107:2/q01/p2", "position": "It marks the causal result of the preceding question's invitation to identify the denier.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī links it to the suspense of the opening question; Elmalılı allows causation; al-Rāzī says denial produces the orphan abuse named after the fāʾ."}, {"id": "107:2/q01/p3", "position": "It is an extra particle.", "reasons": "Al-Akhfash permits omission of fāʾ where Sibawayh requires it and cites 6:121 as parallel."}]}

{"id": "107:2/q06", "question": "What does يدع convey in describing the orphan's treatment?", "turns_on": "The root and vocalization, and whether the concrete shove is understood mainly as physical rebuke, loss of rights, neglect of care, or wider oppression.", "positions": [{"id": "107:2/q06/p1", "position": "It is a forceful, harsh shove or expulsion, often with rebuke or injury.", "reasons": "Al-Farrāʾ, Ibn Qutayba, al-Zajjāj, al-Rāzī, al-Qurṭubī, Ibn ʿĀshūr, Bint al-Shāṭiʾ and Iṣlāḥī compare 52:13, where people are driven into Hell. Al-Jishumī adduces shaking a measure, urging an unsteady person and goats. Ibn ʿAbbās cites Abū Ṭālib's verse for Arab usage; Bint al-Shāṭiʾ favors coercive shove over mere withholding, since Hell's condemned have no denied right, and says payment alone does not excuse rude repulsion. Ibn Jinnī says the lighter reading's shunning remains close to this common sense."}, {"id": "107:2/q06/p2", "position": "It means denying the orphan his due right or property.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, al-Farrāʾ, al-Ṭabarī and many others specify the right; al-Ḍaḥḥāk adds property taken from greed.
